claim: Recovery from sensory deprivation is slow and incomplete in adult visual cortex.
source: Recovery from sensory deprivation is slow and incomplete in adult visual cortex.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract and is supported by citations to prior work (Hubel and Wiesel, 1970; Mitchell and Sengpiel, 2009) in the introduction.

claim: Visual stimulation during locomotion dramatically enhances recovery in the mouse visual cortex after monocular deprivation.
source: In this study, we show that visual stimulation during locomotion, which increases the gain of visual responses in primary visual cortex, dramatically enhances recovery in the mouse.
evidence: This is the primary finding of the study, supported by intrinsic signal imaging data shown in Figure 1 and single unit recording data in Figure 4.

claim: Excitatory neurons regained normal levels of response after visual stimulation during locomotion.
source: Excitatory neurons regained normal levels of response, while narrow-spiking (inhibitory) neurons remained less active.
evidence: This is supported by single unit recording data from broad-spiking cells shown in Figure 4.

claim: Narrow-spiking (inhibitory) neurons remained less active after recovery treatment.
source: Excitatory neurons regained normal levels of response, while narrow-spiking (inhibitory) neurons remained less active.
evidence: This is supported by single unit recording data from narrow-spiking cells shown in Figure 8.

claim: Visual stimulation alone did not enhance recovery from monocular deprivation.
source: Visual stimulation or locomotion alone did not enhance recovery.
evidence: This is supported by intrinsic signal imaging data comparing VS-only group to home-cage controls shown in Figure 1G-I.

claim: Locomotion alone did not enhance recovery from monocular deprivation.
source: Visual stimulation or locomotion alone did not enhance recovery.
evidence: This is supported by intrinsic signal imaging data comparing run-only group to home-cage controls shown in Figure 1G-I.

claim: Recovery is stimulus-specific, with responses recovering only to the particular visual stimuli viewed during locomotion.
source: Responses to the particular visual stimuli viewed by the animal during locomotion recovered, while those to another normally effective stimulus did not, suggesting that locomotion promotes the recovery only of the neural circuits that are activated concurrent with the locomotion.
evidence: This is supported by intrinsic signal imaging data in Figure 3 showing differential recovery for bar vs. noise stimuli depending on which was experienced during running.

claim: Neurons in mouse visual cortex respond with more than two times the number of action potentials during active locomotion than when still.
source: The recent discovery that neurons in mouse visual cortex respond with more than two times the number of action potentials during active locomotion than when still (Niell and Stryker, 2010) led us to test whether this enhanced response might facilitate recovery from the effects of early-onset, long-term monocular visual deprivation (MD).
evidence: This is cited from prior work (Niell and Stryker, 2010).

claim: Monocular deprivation was initiated by suturing shut the right eyelid of C57BL/6 mice early in the critical period (P22–24) and was continued to 4 to 5 months of age.
source: Monocular deprivation was initiated by suturing shut the right eyelid of C57BL/6 mice early in the critical period (P22–24) and was continued to 4 to 5 months of age.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol used in the study.

claim: Mice that experienced visual noise stimulus during daily running (VS+run) showed a remarkable increase in closed-eye responses after only 7 days of binocular vision.
source: In contrast, mice that experienced the noise stimulus during their daily running (VS+run) showed a remarkable increase in closed-eye responses after only 7 days of BV (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This is supported by intrinsic signal imaging data shown in Figure 1C,D.

claim: Control mice kept in standard housing condition showed slow increase in cortical responses to the closed eye over 21 days of binocular vision, remaining well below normal levels.
source: In control mice that were kept in the standard housing condition (home-cage), cortical responses to the closed eye in binocular visual cortex slowly increased over 21d-BV, at which point they were still well below the range of age-matched mice with normal visual experience (Figure 1B,D).
evidence: This is supported by intrinsic signal imaging data shown in Figure 1B,D.

claim: The effect of VS+run on recovery was already significant after 3 days of training.
source: Examined in a separate set of animals, this effect of VS+run was already significant after 3 days of training (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by intrinsic signal imaging data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Responses through the open eye did not change significantly in either VS+run or home-cage groups.
source: Responses through the open eye did not change significantly in either group (Figure 1B,C,E).
evidence: This is supported by intrinsic signal imaging data shown in Figure 1B,C,E.

claim: The ocular dominance index recovered much more rapidly in animals with visual experience during running than in controls.
source: As a result, the ocular dominance index (ODI), computed as a normalized difference between responses to two eyes, recovered much more rapidly in animals with visual experience during running than in controls (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by intrinsic signal imaging data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Recovery using reverse occlusion was similarly enhanced by VS+run.
source: Recovery using reverse occlusion (switching the eye closure) instead of BV was similarly enhanced by VS+run (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by intrinsic signal imaging data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Running velocity and duration were similar between run-only and VS+run groups.
source: Running velocity and duration were similar between run-only and VS+run groups (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: VS+run enhanced recovery of monocular visual areas.
source: VS+run enhanced recovery of monocular visual areas as well (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by intrinsic signal imaging data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The effect of VS+run on monocular areas was rapid.
source: This effect was rapid (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and was particularly prominent for a secondary monocular area, where the home cage and the run-only groups showed no significant improvement even after 21 days of BV.
evidence: This is supported by intrinsic signal imaging data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Home cage and run-only groups showed no significant improvement in secondary monocular area even after 21 days of binocular vision.
source: This effect was rapid (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and was particularly prominent for a secondary monocular area, where the home cage and the run-only groups showed no significant improvement even after 21 days of BV.
evidence: This is stated in the text describing results from Figure 2.

claim: Mice that experienced bar stimuli during running showed significantly greater recovery of closed-eye responses to bars than to noise.
source: Mice that experienced barVS+run showed significantly greater recovery of closed-eye responses to bars than to noise (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by intrinsic signal imaging data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Mice that experienced noise during running showed significantly greater recovery of response to noise than to bars.
source: Likewise, mice that experienced noiseVS+run showed significantly greater recovery of response to noise than to bars (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by intrinsic signal imaging data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Responses to the stimulus that was not experienced during running were similar to those in control mice presented with a blank screen during running.
source: Responses to the stimulus that was not experienced during running were similar to those in control mice presented with a blank screen during running.
evidence: This is stated in the text describing results from Figure 3.

claim: Enhanced recovery is stimulus-specific and suggests that only the specific visual cortical circuits that are active during locomotion recover.
source: These observations reveal that enhanced recovery is stimulus-specific and suggest that only the specific visual cortical circuits that are active during locomotion recover.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the stimulus-specific recovery data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Broad-spiking, presumed excitatory cells constitute approximately 80% of the recordings.
source: We first describe results from the broad-spiking, presumed excitatory cells that constitute ∼80% of the recordings.
evidence: This is stated in the text describing the single unit recording results.

claim: Closed-eye responses in mice that viewed visual stimuli while running during 7 days of binocular vision recovered significantly from their profoundly decreased level after long-term monocular deprivation, in a stimulus-specific manner.
source: Consistent with the intrinsic signal observations as described above, closed-eye responses in mice that viewed visual stimuli while running during 7d-BV recovered significantly from their profoundly decreased level after long-term monocular deprivation (LTMD), in a stimulus-specific manner (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplements 1, 2).
evidence: This is supported by single unit recording data shown in Figure 4 and supplements.

claim: Closed-eye responses to the optimal grating were most increased in grating+run mice among groups.
source: Closed-eye responses to the optimal grating (preferred orientation and spatial frequency) were most increased in grating+run mice among groups (Figure 4B), while responses to contrast-modulated noise were improved most in noise+run mice (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by single unit recording data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Responses to contrast-modulated noise were improved most in noise+run mice.
source: Closed-eye responses to the optimal grating (preferred orientation and spatial frequency) were most increased in grating+run mice among groups (Figure 4B), while responses to contrast-modulated noise were improved most in noise+run mice (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by single unit recording data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Open-eye responses did not differ among four groups of monocularly deprived mice.
source: Open-eye responses did not differ among four groups of monocularly deprived mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by single unit recording data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Ocular dominance recovered to normal levels with stimulus specificity.
source: As a result, ocular dominance recovered to normal levels with similar stimulus specificity (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: This is supported by single unit recording data shown in Figure 4B,C.

claim: In normal animals, the majority of cells in layers 2–4 are orientation-selective (OSI >0.5).
source: In normal animals, the majority of cells in layers 2–4 are orientation-selective (OSI >0.5, Figure 5A,B) and the OSI for the two eyes is similar in each binocular cell (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by single unit recording data shown in Figure 5A,B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The OSI for the two eyes is similar in each binocular cell in normal animals.
source: In normal animals, the majority of cells in layers 2–4 are orientation-selective (OSI >0.5, Figure 5A,B) and the OSI for the two eyes is similar in each binocular cell (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by single unit recording data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Closed-eye OSIs and the binocular correlation of OSI were significantly improved only in grating+run mice but not in other groups.
source: Closed-eye OSIs and the binocular correlation of OSI were significantly improved only in grating+run mice but not in other groups (Figure 5A,B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by single unit recording data shown in Figure 5A,B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Prolonged monocular deprivation caused mismatch of the preferred orientation of two eyes.
source: Prolonged MD caused mismatch of the preferred orientation of two eyes (Figure 5C,D), consistent with requirement of binocular visual experience during the critical period to develop orientation matching (Wang et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by single unit recording data shown in Figure 5C,D and is consistent with cited prior work (Wang et al., 2010).

claim: 7 days of binocular vision improved binocular matching almost to normal levels in grating+run but not in home-cage or noise+run mice.
source: 7d-BV improved binocular matching almost to normal levels in grating+run but not in home-cage or noise+run, mice (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: This is supported by single unit recording data shown in Figure 5C,D.

claim: The distribution of the preferred spatial frequency in closed-eye responses was almost normalized in grating+run mice but not in home-cage or noise+run mice.
source: In addition, the distribution of the preferred spatial frequency in closed-eye responses was almost normalized in grating+run mice but not in home-cage or noise+run mice. (Figure 5E,F).
evidence: This is supported by single unit recording data shown in Figure 5E,F.

claim: Shifts in preferred spatial frequency may account for improvements in behaviorally measured acuity.
source: Such shifts in preferred spatial frequency may account for improvements in behaviorally measured acuity (Mitchell and Sengpiel, 2009).
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observed changes in spatial frequency preference, with reference to prior work (Mitchell and Sengpiel, 2009).

claim: Contrast sensitivity was significantly impaired after long-term monocular deprivation.
source: Contrast sensitivity was significantly impaired after LTMD and was restored almost completely in noise+run mice but not in gratings+run mice (Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by single unit recording data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Contrast sensitivity was restored almost completely in noise+run mice but not in gratings+run mice.
source: Contrast sensitivity was significantly impaired after LTMD and was restored almost completely in noise+run mice but not in gratings+run mice (Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by single unit recording data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Narrow-spiking cells are thought to correspond to inhibitory, predominantly fast-spiking, interneurons.
source: Narrow-spiking cells are thought to correspond to inhibitory, predominantly fast-spiking, interneurons (McCormick et al., 1985; Bartho et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to prior work (McCormick et al., 1985; Bartho et al., 2004).

claim: Spontaneous activity of narrow-spiking cells was greatly reduced after long-term monocular deprivation and did not change significantly after 7 days of binocular vision regardless of the treatment.
source: First, spontaneous activity of narrow-spiking cells was greatly reduced after LTMD and did not change significantly after 7d-BV regardless of the treatment (Figure 7C,D), whereas those of broad-spiking cells were elevated after LTMD and significantly decreased toward normal level in mice after 7d-BV (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: This is supported by single unit recording data shown in Figure 7C,D.

claim: Spontaneous activity of broad-spiking cells was elevated after long-term monocular deprivation and significantly decreased toward normal level in mice after 7 days of binocular vision.
source: First, spontaneous activity of narrow-spiking cells was greatly reduced after LTMD and did not change significantly after 7d-BV regardless of the treatment (Figure 7C,D), whereas those of broad-spiking cells were elevated after LTMD and significantly decreased toward normal level in mice after 7d-BV (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: This is supported by single unit recording data shown in Figure 7A,B.

claim: Opposite changes in spontaneous firing between broad- and narrow-spiking cells may reflect a homeostatic mechanism that alters excitatory–inhibitory balance to maintain cortical activity during prolonged deprivation.
source: These opposite changes in spontaneous firing between broad- and narrow-spiking cells may reflect a homeostatic mechanism that alters excitatory–inhibitory balance to maintain cortical activity during prolonged deprivation.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observed opposite changes in spontaneous firing rates.

claim: Recovery of closed-eye responses and ocular dominance to the gratings in narrow-spiking cells was only modest even in grating+run mice.
source: Second, recovery of closed-eye responses and ocular dominance to the gratings in narrow-spiking cells was only modest even in grating+run mice (Figure 8A, Figure 8—figure supplement 1A), whereas it was nearly complete in broad-spiking cells (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by single unit recording data shown in Figure 8A and Figure 8—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Responses of narrow-spiking cells to contrast-modulated noise through the deprived eye and ocular dominance were incompletely restored both in noise+run and grating+run mice to similar extents, showing no preference for the experienced stimulus.
source: Third, responses of narrow-spiking cells to contrast-modulated noise through the deprived eye and ocular dominance were incompletely restored both in noise+run and grating+run mice to similar extents, showing no preference for the experienced stimulus (Figure 8B, Figure 8—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by single unit recording data shown in Figure 8B and Figure 8—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Responses of narrow-spiking cells through the open-eye were not elevated after long-term monocular deprivation either to the noise or grating stimulus, and did not change significantly in any of 7 days binocular vision mice.
source: Fourth, responses of narrow-spiking cells through the open-eye were not elevated after LTMD either to the noise or grating stimulus, and did not change significantly in any of 7d-BV mice (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by single unit recording data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: The lack of potentiation of open-eye responses during long-term monocular deprivation in narrow-spiking cells may contribute to potentiation of those in broad-spiking cells.
source: This lack of potentiation of open-eye responses during LTMD in narrow-spiking cells may contribute to potentiation of those in broad-spiking cells.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observed differences between narrow- and broad-spiking cells.

claim: The responses of narrow-spiking cells after long-term monocular deprivation suggest that deprivation reduces intracortical inhibition.
source: The responses of narrow-spiking cells after LTMD suggest that deprivation reduces intracortical inhibition.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the narrow-spiking cell data.

claim: Reduction in intracortical inhibition may provide a starting point that allows meager deprived-eye excitatory pathways of the cortical circuit to drive activity upon re-opening.
source: Such a reduction may provide a starting point that allows meager deprived-eye excitatory pathways of the cortical circuit to drive activity upon re-opening.
evidence: This is a speculation about the functional significance of reduced inhibition.

claim: The incomplete recovery of orientation tuning of broad-spiking cells in spite of nearly full restoration of the magnitudes of responses may result from the very limited recovery in narrow-spiking cells.
source: The incomplete recovery of orientation tuning of broad-spiking cells in spite of nearly full restoration of the magnitudes of responses may result from the very limited recovery in narrow-spiking cells, as inhibition is critical for generation of sharp orientation tuning in upper layer neurons in the primary visual cortex (Liu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observed incomplete recovery of orientation tuning and the known role of inhibition in orientation tuning, with citation to prior work (Liu et al., 2011).

claim: Recovery in adulthood from amblyopia induced by monocular visual deprivation during early life is slow and far from complete, even weeks after opening the deprived eye.
source: Recovery in adulthood from amblyopia induced by monocular visual deprivation during early life is slow and far from complete, even weeks after opening the deprived eye (Hubel and Wiesel, 1970; Mitchell and Sengpiel, 2009).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to prior work (Hubel and Wiesel, 1970; Mitchell and Sengpiel, 2009).

claim: Locomotion dramatically enhances the recovery of visual responses, almost to normal levels within a week.
source: In this study, we have used intrinsic signal imaging and single cell recording to find that locomotion, which is known to increase visual responses (Niell and Stryker, 2010), dramatically enhances the recovery of visual responses, almost to normal levels within a week.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by data in Figures 1-8.

claim: The recovery of response was specific to the particular visual stimuli presented during locomotion.
source: Surprisingly, the recovery of response was specific to the particular visual stimuli presented during locomotion.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 3.

claim: Neither locomotion alone nor visual stimulation alone promoted recovery.
source: Neither locomotion alone nor visual stimulation alone promoted recovery.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1G-I.

claim: Recovery is facilitated only in the neural circuits that are activated during running.
source: These findings suggest that recovery is facilitated only in the neural circuits that are activated during running.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the stimulus-specific recovery findings.

claim: Dark exposure has been reported to enhance adult plasticity.
source: Other manipulations have been reported to enhance adult plasticity (Bavelier et al., 2010), such as dark exposure (He et al., 2007), environmental enrichment (Sale et al., 2007), and antidepressant treatment (Maya Vetencourt et al., 2008).
evidence: This is cited from prior work (He et al., 2007).

claim: Environmental enrichment has been reported to enhance adult plasticity.
source: Other manipulations have been reported to enhance adult plasticity (Bavelier et al., 2010), such as dark exposure (He et al., 2007), environmental enrichment (Sale et al., 2007), and antidepressant treatment (Maya Vetencourt et al., 2008).
evidence: This is cited from prior work (Sale et al., 2007).

claim: Antidepressant treatment has been reported to enhance adult plasticity.
source: Other manipulations have been reported to enhance adult plasticity (Bavelier et al., 2010), such as dark exposure (He et al., 2007), environmental enrichment (Sale et al., 2007), and antidepressant treatment (Maya Vetencourt et al., 2008).
evidence: This is cited from prior work (Maya Vetencourt et al., 2008).

claim: Treatments that enhance adult plasticity have in common a decrease in intracortical inhibition.
source: These treatments have in common a decrease in intracortical inhibition, consistent with our finding of reduced activity of inhibitory neurons.
evidence: This is an interpretation connecting prior findings to the current study's observations.

claim: Active hunting by barn owls dramatically increases adaptive plasticity of the auditory map in the superior colliculus.
source: Interestingly, active hunting by barn owls, flying rather than walking or running in this case, dramatically increases adaptive plasticity of the auditory map in the superior colliculus (Bergan et al., 2005).
evidence: This is cited from prior work (Bergan et al., 2005).

claim: Locomotion may induce activity in neuromodulatory circuits that might enhance cortical function or plasticity.
source: Locomotion may induce activity in neuromodulatory circuits that might enhance cortical function or plasticity (Carcea and Froemke, 2013), and it may also produce hemodynamic changes that might affect the operation of the cortical circuit (Seifert and Secher, 2011).
evidence: This is a speculation about potential mechanisms, with citations to relevant prior work (Carcea and Froemke, 2013; Seifert and Secher, 2011).

claim: Locomotion may produce hemodynamic changes that might affect the operation of the cortical circuit.
source: Locomotion may induce activity in neuromodulatory circuits that might enhance cortical function or plasticity (Carcea and Froemke, 2013), and it may also produce hemodynamic changes that might affect the operation of the cortical circuit (Seifert and Secher, 2011).
evidence: This is a speculation about potential mechanisms, with citation to relevant prior work (Seifert and Secher, 2011).

claim: The stimulus specificity of enhanced recovery rules out any general explanation of recovery as an increase in cortical response to any stimulus.
source: The stimulus specificity of enhanced recovery, however, rules out any general explanation of recovery as an increase in cortical response to any stimulus.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the stimulus-specific recovery findings.

claim: The larger responses of the cortical neurons themselves during locomotion would be expected to enhance recovery through the operation of any Hebbian or spike-timing based plasticity mechanism that depends on neural activity.
source: Most simply, the larger responses of the cortical neurons themselves during locomotion would be expected to enhance recovery through the operation of any Hebbian or spike-timing based plasticity mechanism that depends on neural activity (Feldman, 2009).
evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism of enhanced recovery, with citation to relevant prior work (Feldman, 2009).

claim: Plasticity of excitatory connections would be further enhanced by the opposite changes in spontaneous firing of broad- and narrow-spiking neurons.
source: Plasticity of excitatory connections would be further enhanced by the opposite changes in spontaneous firing of broad- and narrow-spiking neurons.
evidence: This is a speculation about how the observed changes in spontaneous firing might contribute to plasticity.

claim: The fictive longitudinal data show that noise stimulation increased the responses of neurons originally responding better to noise more than it did for the neurons that responded better to grating, and vice versa.
source: Indeed, the fictive longitudinal data show that noise stimulation increased the responses of neurons originally responding better to noise more than it did for the neurons that responded better to grating, and vice versa (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The findings are consistent with the Hebbian hypothesis.
source: These findings are consistent with the Hebbian hypothesis.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: It is unknown whether neuronal responses or plasticity are enhanced by locomotion in human visual cortex.
source: In human visual cortex, it is unknown whether neuronal responses or plasticity are enhanced by locomotion.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge.

claim: In monkeys, attention modulates the gain of cortical responses in higher visual areas, but these effects are very much smaller in V1 and smaller than those of locomotion in mice.
source: In monkeys, attention modulates the gain of cortical responses in higher visual areas, but these effects are very much smaller in V1 and smaller than those of locomotion in mice (Maunsell and Cook, 2002; Reynolds and Chelazzi, 2004).
evidence: This is cited from prior work (Maunsell and Cook, 2002; Reynolds and Chelazzi, 2004).

claim: Contrast-modulated stochastic noise matched to the spatiotemporal frequency response of the mouse drives nearly all cells in the primary visual cortex to some extent.
source: We used contrast-modulated stochastic noise matched to the spatiotemporal frequency response of the mouse as the visual stimulus because it drives nearly all cells in the primary visual cortex to some extent (Niell and Stryker, 2008).
evidence: This is cited from prior work (Niell and Stryker, 2008).

claim: Binocular visual experience during the critical period is required to develop orientation matching.
source: Prolonged MD caused mismatch of the preferred orientation of two eyes (Figure 5C,D), consistent with requirement of binocular visual experience during the critical period to develop orientation matching (Wang et al., 2010).
evidence: This is cited from prior work (Wang et al., 2010).

claim: Inhibition is critical for generation of sharp orientation tuning in upper layer neurons in the primary visual cortex.
source: The incomplete recovery of orientation tuning of broad-spiking cells in spite of nearly full restoration of the magnitudes of responses may result from the very limited recovery in narrow-spiking cells, as inhibition is critical for generation of sharp orientation tuning in upper layer neurons in the primary visual cortex (Liu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is cited from prior work (Liu et al., 2011).

claim: Perception in humans can be strengthened by training in an experience-specific manner.
source: Perception in humans can be strengthened by training in an experience-specific manner (reviewed in Sagi, 2011), and responses in mouse visual cortex are reported to do so as well (Frenkel et al., 2006).
evidence: This is cited from prior work (Sagi, 2011).

claim: Responses in mouse visual cortex can be strengthened by training in an experience-specific manner.
source: Perception in humans can be strengthened by training in an experience-specific manner (reviewed in Sagi, 2011), and responses in mouse visual cortex are reported to do so as well (Frenkel et al., 2006).
evidence: This is cited from prior work (Frenkel et al., 2006).

claim: Depriving one eye of normal patterned vision during early life causes a loss of visual acuity (amblyopia).
source: Depriving one eye of normal patterned vision during early life causes a loss of visual acuity (amblyopia) and neurons in the visual cortex lose responsiveness through the deprived eye.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Neurons in the visual cortex lose responsiveness through the deprived eye after monocular deprivation during early life.
source: Depriving one eye of normal patterned vision during early life causes a loss of visual acuity (amblyopia) and neurons in the visual cortex lose responsiveness through the deprived eye.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: If abnormal vision is left uncorrected, recovery of visual function in adulthood is slow and incomplete, both in humans and in higher mammals.
source: If such abnormal vision is left uncorrected, recovery of visual function in adulthood is slow and incomplete, both in humans and in higher mammals, reflecting the limited plasticity of mature cortex (Hubel and Wiesel, 1970; Mitchell and Sengpiel, 2009).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to prior work (Hubel and Wiesel, 1970; Mitchell and Sengpiel, 2009).

claim: The limited recovery of visual function in adulthood reflects the limited plasticity of mature cortex.
source: If such abnormal vision is left uncorrected, recovery of visual function in adulthood is slow and incomplete, both in humans and in higher mammals, reflecting the limited plasticity of mature cortex (Hubel and Wiesel, 1970; Mitchell and Sengpiel, 2009).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to prior work (Hubel and Wiesel, 1970; Mitchell and Sengpiel, 2009).

claim: These findings may provide an avenue for improving recovery from amblyopia in humans.
source: These findings may provide an avenue for improving recovery from amblyopia in humans.
evidence: This is a speculation about the potential clinical implications of the findings.
